{{Short description|Result in geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Loomis–Whitney inequality''' is a result in [[geometry]], which in its simplest form, allows one to estimate the "size" of a <math>d</math>-[[dimension]]al set by the sizes of its <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional projections. The inequality has applications in [[incidence geometry]], the study of so-called "lattice animals", and other areas.

The result is named after the [[United States|American]] [[mathematicians]] [[Lynn Harold Loomis]] and [[Hassler Whitney]], and was published in 1949.

==Statement of the inequality==
Fix a dimension <math>d\ge 2</math> and consider the projections

:<math>\pi_{j} : \mathbb{R}^{d} \to \mathbb{R}^{d - 1},</math>
:<math>\pi_{j} : x = (x_{1}, \dots, x_{d}) \mapsto \hat{x}_{j} = (x_{1}, \dots, x_{j - 1}, x_{j + 1}, \dots, x_{d}).</math>

For each 1 ≤ ''j'' ≤ ''d'', let

:<math>g_{j} : \mathbb{R}^{d - 1} \to [0, + \infty),</math>
:<math>g_{j} \in L^{d - 1} (\mathbb{R}^{d -1}).</math>

Then the '''Loomis–Whitney inequality''' holds:

:<math>\left\|\prod_{j=1}^d g_j \circ \pi_j\right\|_{L^{1} (\mathbb{R}^{d })}
 = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} \prod_{j = 1}^{d} g_{j} ( \pi_{j} (x) ) \, \mathrm{d} x \leq \prod_{j = 1}^{d} \| g_{j} \|_{L^{d - 1} (\mathbb{R}^{d - 1})}.</math>

Equivalently, taking <math>f_{j} (x) = g_{j} (x)^{d - 1},</math> we have

:<math>f_{j} : \mathbb{R}^{d - 1} \to [0, + \infty),</math>
:<math>f_{j} \in L^{1} (\mathbb{R}^{d -1})</math>

implying
:<math>\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} \prod_{j = 1}^{d} f_{j} ( \pi_{j} (x) )^{1 / (d - 1)} \, \mathrm{d} x \leq \prod_{j = 1}^{d} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d - 1}} f_{j} (\hat{x}_{j}) \, \mathrm{d} \hat{x}_{j} \right)^{1 / (d - 1)}.</math>

==A special case==
The Loomis–Whitney inequality can be used to relate the [[Lebesgue measure]] of a subset of [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> to its "average widths" in the coordinate directions. This is in fact the original version published by Loomis and Whitney in 1949 (the above is a generalization).<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Loomis |first1=L. H. |last2=Whitney |first2=H. |date=1949 |title=An inequality related to the isoperimetric inequality |url=https://www.ams.org/bull/1949-55-10/S0002-9904-1949-09320-5/ |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=55 |issue=10 |pages=961–962 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1949-09320-5 |issn=0273-0979|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Let ''E'' be some [[measurable set|measurable subset]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> and let

:<math>f_{j} = \mathbf{1}_{\pi_{j} (E)}</math>

be the [[indicator function]] of the projection of ''E'' onto the ''j''th coordinate [[hyperplane]]. It follows that for any point ''x'' in ''E'',

:<math>\prod_{j = 1}^{d} f_{j} (\pi_{j} (x))^{1 / (d - 1)} = \prod_{j = 1}^{d} 1 = 1.</math>

Hence, by the Loomis–Whitney inequality,

:<math>\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} \mathbf 1_E(x) \, \mathrm{d} x = | E | \leq \prod_{j = 1}^{d} | \pi_{j} (E) |^{1 / (d - 1)},</math>

and hence

:<math>| E | \geq \prod_{j = 1}^{d} \frac{| E |}{| \pi_{j} (E) |}.</math>

The quantity

:<math>\frac{| E |}{| \pi_{j} (E) |}</math>

can be thought of as the average width of <math>E</math> in the <math>j</math>th coordinate direction. This interpretation of the Loomis–Whitney inequality also holds if we consider a finite subset of Euclidean space and replace Lebesgue measure by [[counting measure]].

The following proof is the original one<ref name=":0" />

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=  

Overview: We prove it for unions of unit cubes on the integer grid, then take the continuum limit. When <math>d=1, 2</math>, it is obvious. Now induct on <math>d+1</math>. The only trick is to use Hölder's inequality for counting measures.

Enumerate the dimensions of <math>\R^{d+1}</math> as <math>0, 1, ..., d</math>.

Given <math>N</math> unit cubes on the integer grid in <math>\R^{d+1}</math>, with their union being <math>T</math>, we project them to the 0-th coordinate. Each unit cube projects to an integer unit interval on <math>\R</math>. Now define the following:

* <math>I_1, ..., I_k</math> enumerate all such integer unit intervals on the 0-th coordinate.

* Let <math>T_i</math> be the set of all unit cubes that projects to <math>I_i</math>.

* Let <math>N_j</math> be the area of <math>\pi_j(T)</math>, with <math>j = 0, 1, ..., d</math>.

* Let <math>a_i</math> be the volume of <math>T_i</math>. We have <math>\sum_i a_i = N</math>, and <math>a_i \leq N_0</math>.

* Let <math>T_{ij}</math> be <math>\pi_j(T_i)</math> for all <math>j = 1, ..., d</math>.

* Let <math>a_{ij}</math> be the area of <math>T_{ij}</math>. We have <math>\sum_i a_{ij} = N_j</math>.

By induction on each slice of <math>T_i</math>, we have <math>a_i^{d-1}\leq \prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}</math>

Multiplying by <math>a_i \leq N_0</math>, we have <math>a_i^{d}\leq N_0\prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}</math>

Thus
<math display="block">N = \sum_i a_i \leq \sum_i N_0^{1/d} \prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}^{1/d} =  N_0^{1/d} \sum_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}^{1/d}</math>

Now, the sum-product can be written as an integral over counting measure, allowing us to perform Holder's inequality:
<math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}^{1/d} = \int_i \prod_{j=1}^d a_{ij}^{1/d} = \left\|\prod_{j=1}^d a_{\cdot, j}^{1/d}\right\|_1 \leq \prod_j \|a_{\cdot, j}^{1/d}\|_d=\prod_{j=1}^d \left(\sum_{i=1}^k a_{ij}\right)^{1/d}</math>

Plugging in <math>\sum_i a_{ij} = N_j</math>, we get <math>N^d \leq \prod_{j=0}^d N_j</math>
}}

'''Corollary.''' Since <math>2 |\pi_j(E)| \leq |\partial E|</math>, we get a loose [[isoperimetric inequality]]:

<math display="block">|E|^{d-1}\leq 2^{-d}|\partial E|^d</math>Iterating the theorem yields <math>| E | \leq \prod_{1 \leq j < k \leq d} | \pi_{j}\circ \pi_k (E) |^{\binom{d-1}{2}^{-1}}</math> and more generally<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Burago |first1=Yurii D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gpz6CAAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 |title=Geometric Inequalities |last2=Zalgaller |first2=Viktor A. |date=2013-03-14 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-662-07441-1 |pages=95 |language=en}}</ref><math display="block">| E | \leq \prod_j | \pi_{j} (E) |^{\binom{d-1}{k}^{-1}}</math>where <math>\pi_j</math> enumerates over all projections of <math>\R^d</math> to its <math>d-k</math> dimensional subspaces.

==Generalizations==
The Loomis–Whitney inequality is a special case of the [[Brascamp–Lieb inequality]], in which the projections ''π<sub>j</sub>'' above are replaced by more general [[linear map]]s, not necessarily all mapping onto spaces of the same dimension.
